data.rationale: FND-006 is the clear match. It names all three required items: the ACQ-TH1 file arrives at 06:30 ICT, which is 07:30 SGT; 60 minutes of matching and report generation pushes publication to about 08:30 SGT, after the 08:00 SGT deadline in NFR-8; and 2027 volume is about twice the 2025 level. It also cites Section 16.2 and NFR-8, which overlap the flaw's location. FND-007 is only a weak backup: it mentions NFR-8, but it is about the 99.9% auto-match target being hurt by gaps in the state machine, which is a different defect.

FND-002 is the clear match for F01. It says the Fraud Hook detokenises the full PAN in 13.1 using the Card Adapter's role and sends it to FRV-1. It says this contradicts P2, the 12.1 detokenise restriction and the 12.2 out-of-scope classification. It also covers the P9 breach, the NFR-5 boundary failure and FRV-1 receiving cardholder data. FND-016 is only a weak, related candidate. It covers personal data sent to FRV-1, but under privacy law (NFR-7), not PCI scope or PAN. The other findings are about unrelated defects.

FND-005 is the clear match. It cites NFR-4 (RPO = 0 including region loss) and Section 20.2, where replication is asynchronous with "typical lag under one second". It concludes that commits inside the lag window are lost on unplanned failover, which contradicts the requirement. That covers c1, c2 and c3 at compatible locations (2.2, 20.2, the NFR-4 game day). FND-018 only says the NFR-4 limitations are covered in FND-005. FND-010 only notes that the DR game day is late in the schedule. Neither states the contradiction. They are kept as weak fallbacks.

FND-012 targets the Section 9.3 claim that one partition sustains 10,000 WCU, the merchant_id partition key that puts the largest merchant's traffic on one key, the 4 KB item size missing from the WCU count, and the LSI item-collection limit. It calls the limit unverified rather than stating 1,000 WCU. FND-013 only mentions DynamoDB throttling in Section 9.2 in passing; its defect is orphaned locks and fail-open/fail-closed behaviour, so it is a weak candidate.

FND-004 is the only finding about keeping the encrypted CVC until settlement or for 72 hours under the cited PCI DSS 3.2.1/3.3.2 (NFR-6, Section 12.4). It also points out that incremental authorizations happen after authorization has completed. However, it calls the reading "unverified" and does not clearly say the clauses forbid this retention, so the later scoring step may give only partial credit. None of the other findings is about CVC or sensitive-authentication-data retention.

FND-009 states the whole core insight at the flaw's locations (18.2, 18.3, 18.4, FR-13). It says MFA is optional for Finance (c1). It says Finance can change the payout account and issue refunds (c2). It says a phished Finance password alone can redirect all of a merchant's payouts, with the only confirmation email going to the attacker (c3). It also cites the P9 conflict. No other finding covers the merchant admin plane's payout-account change controls. FND-019 mentions payouts, but it is about how reserves and negative balances are handled, which is a different defect.

FND-011 states the flaw directly. It says the '<1% cascade' premise in 21.1 contradicts the 3.8% retryable rate in 10.5, that a 2,500 ms timeout alone exceeds NFR-2's 1,500 ms, and that NFR-2 would fail its own acceptance test. FND-003 is only related: it covers the same cascade-after-timeout area (11.2) but describes a different defect (duplicate authorizations, not latency).

FND-016 is the only finding that touches data residency. It says all markets' data is processed in Singapore with disaster recovery in Jakarta, and that the evidence register leaves open whether Indonesian or other rules require local processing. It cites NFR-7 and Section 19.1, which are both in the flaw's location. The risk is that it is framed mainly around privacy under NFR-7, which the key's distractor note excludes, so it needs checking. No other finding is about residency or localisation.

FND-001 is a direct match. It says the Redis key idem:resp:{idempotency_key} leaves out merchant_id. It cites Section 9.1, which notes that merchants often use order IDs as keys. It also gives the result: one merchant's payment data leaks to another and the second payment is never created. FND-018 only mentions cross-merchant key reuse in passing, as a missing test that points back to FND-001. FND-013 covers the same idempotency area but describes different failure paths.

FND-008 covers the same defect as F11. It names the single HSM in ap-southeast-1a as a single point of failure, says the missing DEK caching makes every tokenise and detokenise call depend on the HSM so card acceptance stops, and shows that the 1,500 TPS trigger never fires because 55% of 2,000 is 1,100 TPS. It also cites NFR-3 and the three-AZ posture in Section 20.1. It does not cite AWS's two-HSM guidance as fact, though; it only says that guidance is unverified in the register. FND-020 is only loosely related: it mentions the HSM capacity trigger, but as a process with no named owner, not as an availability defect.

FND-017 is a direct candidate for F12. It covers FR-8, 10.3, 2.1 and 26.1. It says the 2% is ambiguous between percentage points and relative percent, which gives c1 and c3. It also says the FR-8 test never exercises the bound. It only partly covers c2, the per-transaction prior versus the merchant-level realised rate: it quotes the weekly merchant-level review but argues a different conflict, between 10.2's weighted score and 10.3. FND-020 is a weak candidate. It cites the 10.3 weekly Routing Review, but its defect is the lack of named owners, not the ambiguity of the tolerance. No other finding deals with FR-8.

FND-018 makes the core point directly. The FR-5 test in 26.1 resends only after the first response arrives, so it never exercises the concurrent duplicates that FR-5 explicitly names. It doesn't spell out a parallel-injection remedy, but the substance is there. FND-013 and FND-001 cover nearby FR-5 idempotency defects, such as orphan locks and Redis scoping, but they don't say the acceptance test is inadequate.

Only FND-014 describes this defect. It says the network tokens are a confirmed decision 'from launch' and that Phase 3 is marked 'No - ready' (c1). It cites Backlog item 2, where Token Requestor registration, the agreement and certification have not started (c2). It concludes that the decision and the readiness rating are overstated (c3). Its location is Section 24 / FR-14, which overlaps the flaw's location. No other finding is about network tokens or TRID.

FND-003 states the core insight at the flaw's locations (11.1, 11.2, FR-7). It treats a timeout as an ambiguous outcome whose late response may be an approval, says cascading leads to a second authorization, and notes that discarding the late approval leaves an orphaned hold with no reversal. It also refutes the claim that cascading cannot create a duplicate charge. FND-013 is only related: it cites the 20.3 sweeper's AUTHORISING-only scope, but for idempotency locks. FND-011 is only related: it covers cascades and the timeout, but its defect is the latency budget.

scores.rationale: States the full timing contradiction: "ACQ-TH1's file lands at 06:30 ICT, which is 07:30 SGT", then "matcher plus report generation take 60 minutes... earliest publication is 08:30 SGT even at today's volume", and "2027 daily attempts are about twice the 2025 level". Cites 16.2 and NFR-8.
Touches settlement and NFR-8 through the state machine ("cannot be settled... counts against the NFR-8 99.9% auto-match target"). This is a different mechanism: there is no timing arithmetic.
About the NFR-2 card authorization latency budget and cascades. Unrelated to the settlement report deadline.
About the FR-5, FR-12 and NFR-9 acceptance tests. Unrelated to NFR-8 timing.
About the network token TRID dependency for AD-010. Unrelated.
About the NFR-7 privacy data inventory. Unrelated.
About NFR-4 RPO zero and asynchronous replication. Unrelated.
About PCI rules on keeping the CVC. Unrelated.

States the Fraud Hook 'detokenise[s] the full card number using the Card Adapter's client library and service role, and send it to the third-party vendor FRV-1', which contradicts 12.2 'Token, BIN, last 4 only', P2 and 12.1. It gives the consequences: 'The NFR-5 assessment against the Section 12.2 CDE boundary would not hold' and 'FRV-1 would receive cardholder data'. It also notes that sharing the role 'breaks P9'. It does not say outright that the Fraud Hook falls inside the CDE or that FRV-1 becomes a third-party service provider, but it describes both in substance.

This is about CVC retention 'until settlement' under 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 in Section 12.4. It shares the PCI/NFR-5 topic but is a different defect: it says nothing about the Fraud Hook handling the PAN or about the scope boundary.

It mentions data sent to FRV-1 ('device fingerprint, IP address, hashed email and phone'), but the defect is a missing privacy data inventory and retention map under NFR-7. It is not about the PAN or CDE scope.

States the Fraud Hook 'detokenise[s] the full card number using the Card Adapter's client library and service role, and send[s] it to the third-party vendor FRV-1'. It says this contradicts P2, 12.1 and 12.2 ('Token, BIN, last 4 only'). The consequence is stated in substance: 'NFR-5 assessment against the Section 12.2 CDE boundary would not hold' and 'FRV-1 would receive cardholder data'. Locations 13.1, 12.1 and 12.2 overlap the flaw's.
About keeping the CVC until settlement under 3.2.1/3.3.2 (12.4, NFR-6). This is a different defect in a different section. It says nothing about the Fraud Hook receiving the PAN.

Covers the privacy data inventory and cross-border transfer under NFR-7. It mentions data sent to FRV-1 ('device fingerprint, IP address, hashed email'), but not the PAN or the CDE scope. So it shares the topic of data sent to FRV-1 but describes a different defect.

States "ACQ-TH1's file lands at 06:30 ICT, which is 07:30 SGT", "matcher plus report generation take 60 minutes... earliest publication is 08:30 SGT even at today's volume", and "2027 daily attempts are about twice the 2025 level". Cites 16.2, 2.2 and NFR-8.
About the network token TRID dependency for AD-010. It has nothing to do with settlement report timing.
About RPO zero versus asynchronous replication (NFR-4). Unrelated to the NFR-8 timing.
About CVC retention under PCI DSS. Unrelated.
Mentions NFR-8 only through the auto-match rate ("counts against the NFR-8 99.9% auto-match target"). The defect it describes is a state-machine gap, not the report publication timing.
Cites 26.2, but only for NFR-9, FR-5 and FR-12 acceptance tests. The NFR-8 timing is not mentioned.
About the card authorization latency budget and cascades (NFR-2). Not settlement timing.
About the personal-data inventory for NFR-7. Unrelated.

States that NFR-4 'requires zero RPO ... on loss of an AWS region' while the 'only cross-region copy is asynchronous with typical lag under one second, so commits inside the lag window are lost'. It challenges AD-004 against NFR-4 and notes that the game day cannot demonstrate zero loss. Its locations are 2.2 and 20.2, which overlap the flaw.
Its subject is the FR-5, FR-12 and NFR-9 acceptance tests. It mentions NFR-4 only to say 'NFR-4 limitations are covered in FND-005' and never states the async-replication RPO contradiction.
Covers phase ordering: the card cohort launches 'before ... DR game days'. It mentions NFR-4 only as not yet demonstrated and says nothing about RPO or asynchronous replication.
Covers NFR-7 personal-data inventory and cross-border transfer, a different defect.
Covers CVC retention under PCI DSS 3.2.1 and 3.3.2, which is unrelated.
Covers how the NFR-8 reconciliation timing works, which is unrelated.
Covers the NFR-2 latency budget and cascade rate, which is unrelated to RPO.
Cites section 24, but the defect is that the network-token TRID dependency (AD-010) is not yet in place, not the RPO contradiction.

Quotes the 'single partition sustains up to 10,000 write capacity units' claim but only says 'The register cannot confirm that per-partition limit'. It never states that the real limit is 1,000 WCU / 3,000 RCU, so c1 is missing. It does give the merchant_id hot key for the merchant with '45% of peak traffic' (c2), and says the count 'ignores item size... response_body is up to 4 KB' and the 'item-collection size constraint from the LSI' (c3).
Same idempotency area (9.2). It mentions 'DynamoDB unavailability or throttling' only as an undefined failure mode, not as a capacity miscalculation or a hot partition.
Same section 9.2, but the defect is different: the Redis key 'idem:resp:{idempotency_key}' has no merchant scope. It says nothing about DynamoDB partition limits.
About asynchronous cross-region replication and NFR-4 RPO. It is unrelated to DynamoDB partition capacity.
About the Network Token Requestor registration and AD-010 readiness. Unrelated.
About whether the acceptance tests can demonstrate their requirements (FR-5 concurrency, FR-12, NFR-9 baseline). It does not cover DynamoDB capacity.

Targets the right claim, 'single partition sustaining 10,000 WCU per second', and says the count 'ignores item size, even though response_body is up to 4 KB' and the 'item-collection size constraint from the LSI'. It also ties the merchant_id key to the merchant with '45% of peak traffic'. But it only calls the limit 'unverified' ('if the real limits are lower'). It never states the actual limit of 1,000 WCU per partition, so c1 is missing.

Same idempotency area (9.2). It notes that 'DynamoDB unavailability or throttling' has no defined handling, but it never names the wrong partition limit, the hot merchant_id key or the WCU math. That is generic 'may throttle' territory.
About the Redis key 'idem:resp:{idempotency_key}' not being scoped to merchant and skipping the body-hash check. This is a different defect from DynamoDB partition capacity.
About asynchronous Aurora replication conflicting with zero RPO, and idempotency state not being rebuildable after failover. Unrelated to DynamoDB partition throughput.
About network-token TRID readiness for AD-010. Unrelated.
About weak acceptance tests for FR-5 concurrency, FR-12 and the NFR-9 baseline. It does not address DynamoDB capacity or the hot partition.

States NFR-4 'requires zero RPO ... on loss of an AWS region', the cross-region copy 'is asynchronous with typical lag under one second', so 'commits inside the lag window are lost on unplanned failover' and the game day 'cannot demonstrate zero loss'.
About phase sequencing: the first card cohort goes live 'before ... DR game day' and before 'NFR-4 are demonstrated'. It does not mention asynchronous replication or the RPO contradiction.
About acceptance tests for FR-5, FR-12 and NFR-9. It only says 'NFR-4 limitations are covered in FND-005' and gives no RPO mechanism.
Covers the latency budget and cascade exclusion for NFR-2, a different defect.
Covers the Token Requestor dependency behind AD-010, a different defect, even though it cites section 24.
Covers the NFR-7 privacy inventory and cross-border data, a different defect.
Covers CVC retention under PCI DSS, which is unrelated.
Covers the reconciliation timing for NFR-8, which is unrelated.

States that the 'fewer than 1% of card payments cascade' premise contradicts the 3.8% retryable rate in 10.5. Notes that a 2,500 ms timeout 'already exceeds NFR-2's 1,500 ms on its own' and that NFR-2 'is likely to fail its own acceptance test'. Cites 21.1, 10.5 and NFR-2.

Covers cascade timeouts in 11.2 but describes a different defect: discarded late approvals lead to double authorization ('customers can be authorised twice'). It says nothing about the p99 latency budget.
About retaining the CVC under PCI DSS 3.2.1/3.3.2. Unrelated to latency.
About NFR-4 RPO zero versus asynchronous replication. Unrelated to latency.
About the timing of settlement report publication (NFR-8). Unrelated.
About the personal-data inventory and retention mapping for NFR-7. Unrelated.

Says 21.1 leaves cascades out of the budget because 'fewer than 1% of card payments cascade', 'yet Section 10.5 gives 3.8% retryable outcomes'. Notes that 'any attempt that hits the 2,500 ms timeout already exceeds NFR-2's 1,500 ms', and that NFR-2 'is likely to fail its own acceptance test'. Cites 21.1, 10.5 and NFR-2.

Same area (cascade after a 2,500 ms timeout, 11.2), but the defect is different. It covers orphaned late approvals and double authorization ('customers can be authorised twice'), not the p99 latency claim.
Concerns how long the CVC is kept under PCI DSS. Has nothing to do with latency.
Concerns the deadline for publishing settlement reports (NFR-8). Unrelated.
Concerns the personal-data inventory under privacy law (NFR-7). Unrelated.
Concerns the RPO-zero requirement versus asynchronous replication (NFR-4). Unrelated.

Identifies retention until settlement/72h and use for incremental authorizations 'which happen after the initial authorization has completed'. But it hedges: 'This review cannot confirm or refute the clause and treats it as unverified', and 'If a QSA reads the standard as prohibiting...'. It never says that 3.2.1/3.3.2 do not permit this, and it does not cite Req. 3.3.1/3.3.1.2. The core insight is only partly stated.
Covers reconciliation timing against NFR-8. Unrelated to CVC retention.
Cites section 11.2, but the defect is late approvals after a cascade timeout causing duplicate holds. It has nothing to do with PCI SAD retention.
Covers personal-data privacy and retention mapping under NFR-7, not PCI CVC retention.
Covers the latency budget's cascade premise. Unrelated to CVC retention.
Covers RPO and asynchronous replication. Unrelated.
Covers network-token TRID readiness in section 24. This is a different defect.
Covers acceptance tests for FR-5, FR-12 and NFR-9, not the NFR-6 PCI rule.

Identifies the right defect and location: CVC kept 'until settlement or for up to 72 hours', with incremental auths that 'happen after the initial authorization has completed'. But it hedges: 'This review cannot confirm or refute the clause and treats it as unverified', and 'If a QSA reads the standard as prohibiting retention...'. It never says the cited 3.2.1/3.3.2 do not allow this, and it does not cite Req. 3.3.1/3.3.1.2, so the core insight is only partly there.
About privacy-law data inventory and retention mapping for NFR-7. It has nothing to do with CVC/SAD retention under PCI DSS.
Section 11.2 cascade timeout: late approvals and no reversal path. A different defect from the CVC retention compliance issue.
Acceptance criteria for FR-5, FR-12 and NFR-9. It does not address the NFR-6 test or CVC retention.
Reconciliation timing for NFR-8. Unrelated.
Network token readiness in Section 24 (AD-010). Unrelated to SAD retention.
Latency budget and cascade rate for NFR-2. Unrelated.
RPO zero versus asynchronous replication under NFR-4. Unrelated.

States "MFA is optional for Finance (Section 18.3)", that Finance can change the payout account, and that "A phished Finance password alone can redirect all of a merchant's payouts, and the only alert goes to the attacker". It also notes there is no step-up or second approver. Cites 18.2, 18.3, 18.4 and FR-13.

About network tokens and the Token Requestor registration ("Without a TRID, all card-on-file traffic falls back to PAN"). This has nothing to do with merchant MFA or payout account takeover. It shares section 24 only by coincidence and cites a different decision.
Concerns CVC retention under PCI DSS 3.2.1/3.3.2 ('Keeping the CVC until settlement rests on an unverified reading'). It says nothing about data residency or where Indonesian data is placed.

Notes the design 'processes all markets' data in Singapore with DR in Jakarta' and that 'whether Indonesian or other rules require local processing is unverified in the register'. This touches the residency gap and the need to confirm the rules. However, it is framed mainly as a privacy inventory and NFR-7 gap. It never states plainly that no localisation requirement exists, never cites payment-system regulation and never says data placement may need to change, so the core insight is only partly stated.
About the Token Requestor registration for network tokens ('Without a TRID, all card-on-file traffic falls back to PAN'). It is unrelated to data residency.

About asynchronous replication breaking RPO zero and about rebuilding idempotency state ('commits inside the lag window are lost'). It cites Section 20.2, but the defect has nothing to do with residency or localisation.
About reconciliation timing missing the NFR-8 deadline ('earliest publication is 08:30 SGT'). It is unrelated to residency.

This finding is about the readiness of the network-token Token Requestor ("Without a TRID, all card-on-file traffic falls back to PAN"). It says nothing about MFA or payout account changes. It shares section 24 with the flaw but cites FR-14, not FR-13.

The finding states all three required items. It says "MFA is optional for Finance (Section 18.3)", that a Finance user can change the payout account, and that "A phished Finance password alone can redirect all of a merchant's payouts, and the only alert goes to the attacker". It also names the missing step-up MFA and second approver and the conflict with P9. It cites 18.2, 18.3, 18.4 and FR-13.
About whether PCI DSS 3.2.1/3.3.2 allow keeping the CVC until settlement; nothing on data residency or Indonesian localisation.
About NFR-4 zero RPO against asynchronous Aurora replication ('Replication is storagelevel and asynchronous'); a DR/RPO defect, not residency.
Reconciliation timing for NFR-8 ('matcher starts once all expected files... have been received'); unrelated to residency.
Network-token TRID dependency for AD-010; unrelated to data localisation.

States the design 'processes all markets' data in Singapore with DR in Jakarta' and that 'whether Indonesian or other rules require local processing is unverified in the register'. It frames the gap as a missing privacy/cross-border position under NFR-7 and centres on the data inventory. It does not say outright that no residency/localisation requirement exists (c1).

States the defect in full. The Redis key is "idem:resp:{idempotency_key}, with no merchant_id" and is checked before DynamoDB. "Two merchants that reuse the same order number... collide", so the second merchant gets the first merchant's "payment object (card BIN and last 4, amounts...)" and its own payment "is never created". It also notes that the hash check is skipped and that this "breaks P3 and FR-5".

Only says the FR-5 acceptance test does not exercise "cross-merchant key reuse (see FND-001)". This is a gap in test coverage. It does not describe the Redis key missing the merchant ID or the resulting data leak.

Covers the same idempotency area (sections 9.1 and 9.2, FR-5) but different defects: orphan IN_PROGRESS locks, DynamoDB outage, and keys reused after 24 hours. It says nothing about the Redis key lacking the merchant ID or cross-merchant collisions.

Concerns RPO, asynchronous replication, and idempotency that cannot be rebuilt because the payment table has "no idempotency_key, request hash or merchant_id column". This is a different mechanism from the Redis fast-path key scoping.
Concerns network token / TRID readiness, which has no connection to idempotency key scoping.
This finding is about network tokens and the Token Requestor registration ('Network tokens ... from launch'). It does not discuss the idempotency cache, so it is unrelated.

It states every required item: the key is 'idem:resp:{idempotency_key}, with no merchant_id'. It notes that 'order and invoice numbers' are accepted as keys, so 'Two merchants ... collide'. It gives the consequence: 'the second merchant receives the first merchant's payment object ... and its own payment is never created'. It also covers the skipped 422 check and the breach of P3/FR-5. It cites 9.1 and 9.2.

It is in the idempotency/FR-5 area, but the defect is different: asynchronous replication and rebuilding idempotency state after failover ('payment table has no idempotency_key ... merchant_id column'). It does not mention the Redis key scoping.

It only says the acceptance tests do not cover 'cross-merchant key reuse (see FND-001)'. That is a gap in test coverage, not a statement of the Redis key defect or its consequences, and the cited section is 26.1.

It covers idempotency failure paths: orphan IN_PROGRESS locks, a DynamoDB outage, and order-ID keys reused 'after the 24-hour expiry'. It overlaps 9.1 and 9.2 but never identifies that the Redis key has no merchant scope or the collision between merchants.

Covers all three items: 'no response within 2,500 ms' is classed as retryable, and 'A late approval leaves a live authorization hold ... while the second acquirer also approves'. It also says 'no reversal message, no record of the orphaned authorization' and rebuts the no-duplicate claim. Cites 11.1, 11.2 and FR-7.

Covers the same timeout and cascade area, but the defect is about the latency budget ('Any attempt that hits the 2,500 ms timeout already exceeds NFR-2'). It does not raise duplicate authorization or orphaned approvals.
Covers the retry engine, but the defect is that scheme reattempt limits are never stated. The distractor note says 11.3 scheme controls are not this flaw.
Notes that the sweeper 'scans only payments in AUTHORISING', but only for orphaned idempotency locks. It does not cover timed-out cascade attempts or double authorization.

Mentions that 'Mapping a Vault 503 to a retryable outcome' makes cascades fail, but the defect is the HSM single point of failure. It does not address the ambiguous acquirer outcome or duplicate charges.
Concerns the weakness of the acceptance tests for FR-5, FR-12 and NFR-9, so it is unrelated to the cascade timeout issue.
Concerns idempotency key scoping in the Redis fast path, so it is unrelated.
Concerns network token readiness in section 24, so it is unrelated to the cascade flaw.
Concerns cross-region RPO and asynchronous replication, so it is unrelated.

Covers all three required items: the 2,500 ms timeout is treated as retryable, and "A late approval leaves a live authorization hold ... while the second acquirer also approves". It also notes "no reversal message, no record of the orphaned authorization" and challenges the 'cannot create a duplicate charge' claim. Located at 11.1, 11.2 and FR-7.

Cites 20.3, saying the sweeper "scans only payments in AUTHORISING", but only about orphaned IN_PROGRESS idempotency locks. It does not cover timed-out acquirer attempts or duplicate authorizations from cascading, so the mechanism is different.

Says the scheme reattempt limits are never stated. That is about scheme compliance (11.3), which the key's distractor notes exclude. It says nothing about the ambiguous outcome of a timeout or about orphaned approvals.
About cascades and timeouts breaking the latency budget ("2,500 ms timeout already exceeds NFR-2's 1,500 ms"). This is a latency defect, not duplicate authorization.
About asynchronous cross-region replication versus the zero-RPO requirement. Unrelated to this flaw.
About weak acceptance tests for FR-5, FR-12 and NFR-9. Unrelated to cascading after a timeout.
About a single HSM as a single point of failure. It only touches on a "Vault 503 to a retryable outcome" that makes cascades fail. This is a different defect.
About the Redis idempotency key not being scoped to the merchant. Unrelated.
Cites section 24, but the topic is network-token readiness (AD-010). Unrelated defect.

States the full defect: "every KEK in one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. DEKs are not cached, so every tokenise and detokenise call needs the HSM" (c1, c2), "Losing the HSM or its AZ stops card acceptance... which threatens NFR-3", and the trigger "is never reached... 55% card share of 2,000 TPS is 1,100 TPS" (c3). It also contrasts this with the three-AZ posture in 20.1. Its locations, 12.3, 20.1 and NFR-3, overlap the key's.

It only mentions "the HSM capacity trigger" as a process with no named owner. It does not say there is a single HSM, does not call it a single point of failure, and does not say the trigger never fires. Its locations, the title page and 10.3, do not overlap the key's.
This finding is about the network-token Token Requestor registration and the Phase 3 readiness rating. It has nothing to do with HSM topology or availability.

This finding is about the Fraud Hook detokenising the PAN with the Card Adapter's role, which breaks P2 and the CDE scope. That is an access-control and scope defect, not the single-HSM availability flaw.

States all of it: "one HSM in ap-southeast-1a" is a single point of failure; "DEKs are not cached, so every tokenise and detokenise call needs the HSM"; and "Losing the HSM or its AZ stops card acceptance". It shows the trigger "is never reached ... 55% card share of 2,000 TPS is 1,100 TPS", which "threatens NFR-3" and conflicts with the three-AZ posture. Sections 12.3 and 20.1 overlap the key's locations.

Mentions "the HSM capacity trigger" only as a human process with no named owner. It does not raise the single point of failure or the availability defect. Its locations (title page, 10.3) do not overlap the key's.
Covers the network-token Token Requestor registration not being ready (AD-010). It cites Section 24, but the defect has nothing to do with HSM topology or availability.

Covers the Fraud Hook detokenising the PAN and sending it to FRV-1, which breaks P2 and the CDE scope. It cites Section 12.1, but the defect is about access control and PCI scope, not the single-HSM availability problem.

States the units ambiguity: "Percentage points and a relative 2% differ materially", and "The FR-8 test checks only expected choices and does not probe the bound." It quotes the weekly Routing Review but never states that one reading is a per-transaction prior comparison and the other is a merchant-level realised-rate check. The conflict it raises instead is between 10.2 and 10.3, so c2 is missing.
Cites 10.3 and the weekly Routing Review, but only to say it has "no named owner or SLA". That is a different defect, not the ambiguity of the 2% bound.
About the FR-5, FR-12 and NFR-9 acceptance tests. Nothing on FR-8 or the 2% tolerance.
About scheme reattempt limits under FR-7. Unrelated to the FR-8 routing tolerance.
About state machine transitions and settlement. Unrelated.
About the network-token TRID dependency under AD-010. Unrelated.
About phase sequencing before the Fraud Hook and PCI assessment. Unrelated.
About payout refunds, reserves and negative balances. Unrelated.

States the ambiguity of FR-8's '2%' and the unitless 'tolerance (default 2)', and separates absolute from relative: 'Percentage points and a relative 2% differ materially', 'the FR-8 test checks only expected choices'. It does not raise the per-transaction prior vs weekly merchant-level realised rate reading. data.rationale: The premise checks out. Section 28 puts the first cohort (Singapore, cards and PayNow) live after Phase 7. The Fraud Hook is Phase 8, blocked on the FRV-1 contract (Backlog item 4). The PCI assessment, load, chaos and DR game days and the Section 26 test plan are Phase 9. FR-9 requires every card payment to be scored before authorization, and NFR-5, NFR-1, NFR-2 and NFR-4 are not shown to be met until Phase 9. So live card traffic would run without them. Section 27's conclusion names only the Admin API schemas and disputes as non-blocking gaps and does not consider this. No key flaw (F01–F14) or observation (O01) covers launch sequencing, and no other finding in this review raises it.

The premise is accurate. Section 7.2 allows CAPTURED -> PARTIALLY_REFUNDED|REFUNDED and PARTIALLY_REFUNDED -> REFUNDED, with no transition from either refund state to SETTLED. Section 16.2, however, moves every matched payment to SETTLED, and FR-2 forbids unlisted transitions. A payment refunded before settlement therefore cannot be settled. There is also no CAPTURED->CAPTURED transition, so the multiple partial captures implied by FR-1 are impossible. The memo-ledger wording point (Section 8 step 10 vs Section 14.3) is minor but grounded in the text. None of the key flaws F01-F14 covers the state machine, and Section 7 is not a key sound section. No other finding in the review raises this issue. It is a specific, real gap.

The premise is accurate. §12.4, NFR-6 and the Confirmed Decisions keep the encrypted CVC until SETTLED or for up to 72 hours, use it for incremental authorizations (tips, hotel extensions), and state that PCI DSS v4.0 3.2.1/3.3.2 'allow sensitive authentication data to be retained in encrypted form until the transaction is settled'. The problem is real: PCI DSS forbids keeping SAD after authorization (3.2.1 covers pre-authorization storage, 3.3.2 covers issuers), so NFR-5/NFR-6 are at risk. This is the substance of key flaw F06, though the finding hedges by calling the clause 'unverified'. It is specific and grounded in the document. No other finding in the review covers CVC/SAD retention, and it does not match O01.

The premise checks out against the document. §9.3 says "a single partition sustains up to 10,000 write capacity units per second" and counts "two writes ... or about 1,800 WCU at peak" for M-0001. §9.2 gives response_body "up to 4 KB" and an LSI on created_at. The problem is real: a DynamoDB partition is limited to 1,000 WCU/s, 4 KB writes cost several WCU each, and the LSI's item-collection constraint stops one merchant key from being split. No other finding in the review covers DynamoDB capacity, so it is not a duplicate. It does not match O01, which is about Stripe vs IETF attribution. In substance it is the same defect as key flaw F04. It hedges by calling the limit "unverified", but it is specific and grounded in the document.

The premise is true. Section 11.3 only says the Retry Engine stops "at the scheme limits applicable to the card" and never states those limits, the rule source, or whether a cross-acquirer cascade of 05/91/96 counts as a reattempt. Section 27 still rates the Retry Engine "Ready", claiming "scheme rules specified (Section 11)", and the FR-7 test in 26.1 checks "stop at scheme reattempt limits". This is a specific, document-grounded readiness gap. It is not among the key flaws (F10 is the different timeout/no-reversal issue), and it does not duplicate FND-003 or any other finding.

The premises hold against the document. §9.2 relies on the §20.3 sweeper, which selects payments 'in AUTHORISING for more than 30 seconds'. §20.3 adds that the sweeper 'also completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS', which the finding slightly overlooks, but nothing defines how that works when the pod crashed before a payment row existed or while the payment was in CREATED (fraud or 3DS stage). §20.4 covers a Redis outage but not a DynamoDB outage or throttling, so fail-open versus fail-closed is undefined. §9.1 accepts order IDs as keys and treats a request after the 24-hour expiry as new, a residual FR-5 duplicate risk the document doesn't discuss. These gaps are specific and real. They are not covered by key flaws F04, F09 or F13, and not by other findings: FND-001 is about Redis key scoping, FND-005 about DR rebuild of idempotency state, FND-012 about DynamoDB capacity.

The premise is accurate. FR-8 says 'reduces the expected authorization rate by more than 2%', while Section 10.3 and Section 24 give a unitless 'tolerance (default 2)'. The Section 26.1 FR-8 test only checks that 'the selected acquirer matches the expected choice' and never tests the bound. Percentage points and relative percent are different thresholds (2 points on the 88.1% baseline in Section 10.5 is about 2.3% relative), and Section 10.3's cheapest-vs-highest-approval check can disagree with the cost-weighted score in Section 10.2. The issue is specific, grounded in the document and real. No other finding in this review covers it, and O01 is unrelated (Section 23 attribution).

The premise checks out against the document. NFR-7 requires purpose limitation, retention limits and access logging under five privacy laws. Section 13.1 sends device fingerprint, IP address, user agent, hashed email and phone, and shipping and billing country to FRV-1, whose DPA is still pending (Backlog item 4). FR-15 requires holding customers' nominated bank accounts for payout refunds. Section 19.1 sets retention only for payment and attempt records, idempotency records, webhook events and settlement files, and places all primary data in ap-southeast-1 with Jakarta for DR only. The design gives no field-level purpose and retention map, no data-subject request process and no basis for cross-border transfer, even though the 26.2 acceptance criterion requires every personal data field to be mapped. One small error: the payload carries shipping and billing country, not full addresses. This is specific and grounded in the document. It is not covered by another finding in the review, and it goes beyond F07's residency point.

The premise holds. FR-15 sends some refunds as a bank payout to "the customer's nominated account", but no section says how that account is collected, verified or protected, or how the payout is journaled (14.2 shows only capture, settlement and merchant payout). Section 16.3 subtracts "reserves and pending dispute holds" without defining them, and there is no rule for a negative merchant_payable. Section 27 still rates Payouts "Ready" and cites only 16.3. The finding acknowledges that dispute case management is out of scope and focuses on v1 payout rules, which are in scope because disputes are ingested as ledger events. It is specific, grounded in the document, not in the key, and not covered by any other finding.

The premises check out: the title page cites a draft PCI DSS Scoping Memo and a 2026-09-21 consolidation with no change log, §10.3 has a weekly Routing Review with no owner, and the other processes it lists are in the document. The complaint itself is generic governance advice (name owners and SLAs, keep change control) that fits almost any design. By its own admission it 'does not cause failure by itself', and it identifies no concrete defect in this design. The substantive points it touches, the draft PCI memo and the HSM trigger, are already covered by FND-004 and FND-008.
